newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Glaxo head says prepared for Zantac fall.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo head says prepared for Zantac fall.

text.p: Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc, the world's biggest drugs firm, is prepared for the loss this July of the U.S. patent on its money-spinning Zantac ulcer drug, its chief executive designate said on Wednesday.
"We are prepared... the whole market is prepared," said Sean Lance, who is currently Glaxo's chief operating officer.

Zantac is the drug on which Glaxo swiftly rose to fortune, but the firm is confident it can ride out the inevitable sales collapse that follows the entry into the market of cheaper generic competition after patents lapse.

The firm has been pushing its new products, such as HIV and AIDS treatments Retrovir and Epivir. Though the Zantac fall will most likely see flat profits in 1997 and 1998 the firm is confident it can kick-start growth after that.

"The new products are taking the slack," Lance told reporters during a visit to South Africa. Lance is in South Africa in his role as president of the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Associations.
Earlier this month the firm posted promising trial results on a new drug for treating Hepatitis B which raised market hopes Glaxo may have discovered a new blockbuster.
The firm said advanced studies showed that Lamuvudine may reduce and even reverse liver damage caused by the illness.
But Lance was cautious about some of the ecstatic market reaction. "With something like this you get excited, then you get depressed. We will just have to wait and see," he said.
Lance is to take the helm of the firm from current chief executive Sir Richard Sykes after the firm's annual general meeting in 1998.

The group was born out of the nine billion stg takeover by Glaxo of former rival Wellcome and came at the height of a merger wave that also saw the creation of such firms as Swiss giant Novartis and U.S.-Swedish firm Upjohn Pharmacia .
But Lance said the pace towards mergers in the global industry seemed to have slackened, though the costs of research and development faced by firms were still enormous.
"I wouldn't like to rule (mergers) out, but people will approach them far more circumspectly," he said. -- Paul Harris, Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
